newsitem.title: PERU: Peru peace panel meets to seek end to rebel crisis.
newsitem.headline: Peru peace panel meets to seek end to rebel crisis.

text.p: Members of a peace commission appointed to resolve a six-week-old hostage crisis at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Peru met formally for the first time on Tuesday in a step toward talks with rebel gunmen.

The three-member commission briefed Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori and Japan's point man on the crisis, Terusuke Terada, on "the existing conditions for the eventual development of talks," government negotiator Domingo Palermo told reporters.

The composition of the panel, Red Cross mediator Michel Minnig, Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent and Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, was accepted earlier this month by the government and the Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages.

Efforts to start talks with the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas have stalled over the main rebel demand of freedom for about 400 jailed comrades, which Fujimori has refused to discuss.
The Peruvian government, under pressure from Japan over the handling of the crisis, added on Tuesday that it is considering closer cooperation with Tokyo to help end the siege peacefully.
Japanese authorities expressed concerns to the Peruvian government this week over police manoeuvres outside the diplomatic compound that the MRTA members stormed on Dec. 17.
"In light of this, President Alberto Fujimori is studying the possibilty of closer coordination to iron out details and agree on positions to resolve this peacefully," Palermo said.
Increasingly bold police tactics have heightened alarm in Tokyo, which is particularly concerned about two dozen Japanese nationals held captive.
Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto again called on Peru on Tuesday to tone down troop movements at the site.

"We understand the need to tighten security at the compound but ask that you give sufficient consideration to preventing accidents or incidents," government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama quoted Hashimoto as telling Fujimori by phone.

The MRTA rebels fired several bullets on Monday at police aboard a convoy of armoured cars after officers made obscene gestures toward the residence while parading by. The bullets hit the vehicle, with one narrowly missing a policeman inside.
Even after the shooting, security forces, who had orders not to return fire, continued their manoeuvres in an apparent attempt to crack the resolve of the estimated 15 rebels.
Police have thrown stones and garbage into the diplomatic compound, flown helicopters overhead and trained machine guns on the house, moves the guerrillas considered a provocation.

On Tuesday, Peru blasted military tunes at the ambassador's home from three sets of speakers around the mined and booby-trapped diplomatic compound to drown out revolutionary anthems played by the MRTA captors.
Fujimori, whose brother Pedro is among the captives, has insisted the police moves are not a prelude to an assault but a tightening of security prior to talks and a negotiated exit.

A communique from MRTA prisoners in Lima's Canto Grande prison, sent on Tuesday to Reuters, slammed Fujimori's decision earlier this month to suspend family and Red Cross visits as "arbitrary and abusive."
Amnesty International on Tuesday argued that the hostage taking did not justify what it described as an official violation of the rights of the MRTA prisoners.
Local media reported on Tuesday that police had captured an important leader of the larger Shining Path guerrilla movement in Peru's northern coastal region.

Anti-terrorism police arrested Ciro Carranza in the city of Trujillo, 350 miles (560 km) north of Lima, on Saturday after he was discovered with false identification papers and coded messages, local newspapers said.
Conflicts unleashed by the MRTA and Shining Path have cost at least 30,000 lives and $25 billion in infrastructure damage in Peru since 1980.

The MRTA rebels, who take the name for their movement from an 18th-century Indian leader who led an uprising against Spanish colonial rule, orginally seized hundreds of guests when they stormed a garden party at the residence.

They released most but kept those they consider the most important bargaining chips, including two Peruvian ministers, generals, security chiefs, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats and the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors.
